questions.stem: A 4 year old girl with Down syndrome has had 3 weeks of tiredness, bruising on her legs and two ear infections. She is pale with petechiae, cervical lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. There is a soft systolic murmur. Her temperature is 37.9°C. Her blood film shows lymphoblasts. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A young child with Down syndrome, marrow failure, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and lymphoblasts has ALL, the commonest childhood leukaemia (peak 2 to 5 years).

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: 4 year old girl with Down syndrome
steps.x: Age 2 to 5, Down syndrome, anaemia, bleeding, infection, nodes, organomegaly, lymphoblasts.

elim: Usually affects adults over 65; the film shows lymphoblasts.
Causes pancytopenia without blasts, lymphadenopathy or organomegaly.
Causes isolated thrombocytopenia in a well child, not anaemia, blasts and organomegaly.
Causes atypical lymphocytes, not lymphoblasts with marrow failure.

steps.x: **A. Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.** Child + marrow failure + organomegaly + lymphoblasts = ALL.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man had chemotherapy for lymphoma 6 years ago. He now has 2 weeks of headache, blurred vision and confusion, with nosebleeds and a chest infection. His temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 108 bpm and BP 138/80 mmHg. There is no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. His blood film shows numerous myeloblasts. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A rapidly ill older adult with previous chemotherapy, marrow failure, myeloblasts and features of hyperviscosity (headache, visual disturbance, confusion) has AML.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: had chemotherapy for lymphoma 6 years ago
steps.x: Over 65, previous chemotherapy, short history, marrow failure, myeloblasts, very high WCC with neurological symptoms.

elim: Causes a lymphocytosis of mature cells, often found incidentally.
Has mature myeloid cells at all stages and massive splenomegaly, not a blast crisis picture here.
Causes bone pain, hypercalcaemia and renal failure, not myeloblasts.
Would usually cause lymphadenopathy, not circulating myeloblasts.

steps.x: **A. Acute myeloid leukaemia.** Older adult + acute marrow failure + myeloblasts = AML (risk: previous chemotherapy).

questions.stem: A 47 year old man has 4 months of fatigue, night sweats, weight loss of 7 kg and a dragging feeling in his left upper abdomen. His spleen is palpable to the right iliac fossa. His blood film shows neutrophils, myelocytes and metamyelocytes at all stages with many basophils and eosinophils. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Massive splenomegaly, B symptoms and a very high WCC with myeloid cells at every stage plus basophils is CML.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: palpable to the right iliac fossa
steps.x: Middle-aged, slow history, massive spleen, myeloid cells at all stages, basophilia.

elim: Would show mainly blasts and a short, severe illness, not mature cells at all stages.
Causes a lymphocytosis with smudge cells, not a myeloid picture.
Presents with lymphadenopathy, not a massive myeloid white count.
Does not cause basophilia, massive splenomegaly or a WCC this high without infection.

steps.x: **C. Chronic myeloid leukaemia.** Massive splenomegaly + leukocytosis with all myeloid stages and basophils = CML.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man has noticed painless lumps in his neck and armpits over 6 months. He feels well, with no fevers or weight loss. He has symmetrical, non-tender, rubbery cervical and axillary nodes and a spleen tip. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: An older man who is well, with symmetrical lymphadenopathy and a raised count of mature lymphocytes, has CLL.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Older man, slow and asymptomatic course, symmetrical nodes, lymphocytosis.

elim: A childhood disease with blasts and marrow failure.
Usually younger patients, and it does not cause a lymphocytosis.
Causes a sore throat and atypical lymphocytes in young people.
Causes matted nodes with systemic symptoms, not a lymphocytosis.

steps.x: **B. Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia.** Older man + lymphocytosis + painless nodes, often incidental = CLL.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman has 5 days of gum bleeding, heavy periods and widespread bruises. She is pale with petechiae. Her blood film shows abnormal promyelocytes packed with granules and bundles of Auer rods. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Abnormal promyelocytes with Auer rods and DIC (long PT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer) in a younger adult is acute promyelocytic leukaemia, an AML subtype with t(15;17).

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Bleeding, DIC on the clotting screen, abnormal promyelocytes.

elim: Causes pancytopenia without abnormal promyelocytes or DIC.
A slow illness with a high WCC and massive spleen, not DIC.
Causes isolated thrombocytopenia with normal clotting.
Causes schistocytes with normal PT and fibrinogen.

steps.x: **A. Acute promyelocytic leukaemia.** Promyelocytes + DIC = APML (t(15;17)), an emergency.

questions.stem: A 3 year old boy has had 2 weeks of pallor, tiredness and breathlessness when he runs. His mother has noticed bruises. His blood film shows lymphoblasts. His Hb is 64 g/L (110–140) and platelets 28 ×10⁹/L (150–400). His temperature is 37.6°C and pulse rate 136 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
questions.e: ALL infiltrates the liver, spleen and nodes, so hepatosplenomegaly is common, with pallor and a soft flow murmur from anaemia.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
A young child with marrow failure and lymphoblasts: ALL.

elim: Not a feature of leukaemia.
Classically seen in monocytic AML, not childhood ALL.
A sign of iron deficiency.
Typical of CML, not ALL.

steps.x: **C. Hepatosplenomegaly.** ALL on examination = pallor, bruising, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly.

questions.stem: A 5 year old boy has just been diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. His parents ask about his outlook. His white cell count at diagnosis was 12 ×10⁹/L. Cytogenetics show hyperdiploidy. On examination he has an enlarged, painless left testis.
questions.q: Which feature is most associated with a poorer prognosis?
o: Low white cell count at diagnosis
questions.e: Testicular involvement (and male sex) are recognised poor prognostic factors in boys with ALL; hyperdiploidy is favourable.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Mostly good features, plus one bad: the testis.

elim: Age 1 to 10 years is favourable.
He is male; female sex is the favourable one.
Extra chromosomes in the blasts predict a better prognosis.
A low count is favourable.

steps.x: **E. Testicular involvement.** ALL: testis and male sex = worse; hyperdiploidy, age 1 to 10, low WCC = better.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman is diagnosed with acute myeloid leukaemia. She had radiotherapy and chemotherapy for breast cancer 5 years ago. She also has type 2 diabetes, hypothyroidism and coeliac disease. She has never smoked.
questions.q: Which is the most likely risk factor for her leukaemia?
questions.e: Radiation exposure and previous chemotherapy are recognised causes of leukaemia, alongside genetic disorders such as Down syndrome.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: radiotherapy and chemotherapy for breast cancer
steps.x: An older woman with AML and previous cancer treatment.

elim: Linked to enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma, not AML.
Not a risk factor for leukaemia.
Not a risk factor for leukaemia.
AML is not more common in women.

steps.x: **D. Previous chemotherapy and radiotherapy.** Leukaemia risk factors: radiation, previous chemotherapy, Down syndrome.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man is 12 days into induction chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukaemia. He has shivers and feels unwell. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 116 bpm, BP 98/60 mmHg and respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute. His central line site looks clean. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Fever above 38°C with neutrophils below 0.5 ×10⁹/L during chemotherapy is neutropenic sepsis, a medical emergency.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Mid-chemotherapy, fever, tachycardia, low BP, neutrophils near zero.

elim: Needs a very high blast count; his WCC is very low.
He has not had a recent transfusion.
Occurs in the first days of chemotherapy with high potassium and urate, not fever with neutropenia.
A diagnosis of exclusion; fever with neutrophils below 0.5 is sepsis until proven otherwise.

steps.x: **C. Neutropenic sepsis.** Fever + neutropenia on chemotherapy = neutropenic sepsis.

questions.stem: A 6 year old boy has a painless swelling of his right testis, aching legs and tiredness for 3 weeks. He has cervical lymphadenopathy and bone tenderness. His full blood count shows Hb 82 g/L (110–140), platelets 41 ×10⁹/L (150–400) and lymphoblasts on the film.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Marrow failure, bone pain, lymphadenopathy and lymphoblasts in a child is ALL; testicular infiltration is a recognised site and a poor prognostic factor.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: painless swelling of his right testis
steps.x: Child, cytopenias, bone pain, nodes, testis, lymphoblasts.

elim: Painful, with parotitis, and does not cause blasts or cytopenias.
An adrenal tumour that can infiltrate marrow, but lymphoblasts point to ALL.
Sudden and very painful, with no blood count changes.
A testicular tumour that does not cause marrow failure with lymphoblasts.

steps.x: **A. Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.** Child + lymphoblasts + testis involvement = ALL.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man has a routine blood test before cataract surgery. He feels well. There is no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. His Hb is 138 g/L (130–180), white cell count 22 ×10⁹/L (4.0–11.0), lymphocytes 18 ×10⁹/L (1.0–4.0) and platelets 210 ×10⁹/L (150–400).
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on his blood film?
questions.e: An incidental lymphocytosis in a well older man is CLL; the fragile malignant lymphocytes rupture when the film is made, giving smudge cells.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
An older man, well, isolated lymphocytosis found by chance.

elim: A hallmark of AML blasts.
Seen in G6PD deficiency.
Seen in acute promyelocytic leukaemia.
Seen in lymph node biopsy in Hodgkin lymphoma, not on a blood film.

steps.x: **E. Smudge cells.** CLL on film = smudge (smear) cells; confirm with peripheral blood flow cytometry.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman has 3 weeks of tiredness, mouth ulcers and bruising. Her full blood count shows Hb 76 g/L (115–165), white cell count 2.4 ×10⁹/L (4.0–11.0) and platelets 19 ×10⁹/L (150–400). Her blood film shows occasional blasts. She has no lymphadenopathy.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: Bone marrow biopsy is the gold-standard test that confirms and classifies leukaemia after an FBC and film show blasts.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or confirm before reading the options.
Pancytopenia with circulating blasts.

elim: Used for staging lymphoma, not diagnosing leukaemia.
Checks for CNS disease after diagnosis, not the diagnosis itself.
She has no lymphadenopathy, and it diagnoses lymphoma.
Blasts are already seen; the marrow must be examined to confirm and classify.

steps.x: **A. Bone marrow biopsy.** Suspected leukaemia: FBC and film first, bone marrow biopsy confirms.

questions.stem: A 19 year old man sees his GP with 3 weeks of tiredness, a sore throat that keeps coming back and bruises he cannot explain. He looks pale. His temperature is 37.5°C. There are a few petechiae on his ankles.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
o: Full blood count and blood film
questions.e: Anaemia, recurrent infection and bruising suggest marrow failure, so the first-line test is an FBC with blood film, looking for cytopenias and blasts.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or confirm before reading the options.

clues: sore throat that keeps coming back
steps.x: Marrow failure triad: anaemia, infection, bleeding.

elim: The confirmatory test, done after the FBC and film.
Petechiae suggest low platelets, which needs a full count.
Does not assess marrow failure.
Does not explain bruising, pallor and petechiae.

steps.x: **D. Full blood count and blood film.** First-line in suspected leukaemia = FBC + blood film (urgently).

questions.stem: A 77 year old woman with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia on watch and wait has 2 weeks of breathlessness and dark urine. She is pale and her sclerae are yellow. Her Hb is 72 g/L (115–165), reticulocytes 9% (0.5–2.5), bilirubin 54 µmol/L (<21) and LDH 640 U/L (<250). Her blood film shows spherocytes.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on further investigation?
questions.e: CLL is associated with warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia: spherocytes, reticulocytosis, raised bilirubin and LDH, and a positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or confirm before reading the options.
CLL with haemolysis and spherocytes.

elim: Seen in oxidative haemolysis from G6PD deficiency.
Haemolysis does not cause iron deficiency.
Causes macrocytosis without reticulocytosis.
Fragments from microangiopathic haemolysis, not warm antibodies.

steps.x: **D. Positive direct antiglobulin test.** CLL + haemolysis = warm AIHA = DAT positive.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia for 6 years has 4 weeks of fevers, drenching sweats and weight loss of 6 kg. One node in his left neck has grown from 2 to 6 cm. His LDH is 980 U/L (<250). His temperature is 38.2°C.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
o: Repeat full blood count in 3 months
questions.e: Sudden B symptoms, a rapidly growing node and a high LDH in CLL suggest Richter's transformation to high-grade lymphoma, confirmed by lymph node biopsy.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or confirm before reading the options.
Long-standing CLL, sudden deterioration, one fast-growing node.

elim: The marrow already shows CLL; the node shows whether it has transformed.
Tests for autoimmune haemolysis, which this is not.
Will just confirm CLL again.
Sudden deterioration needs urgent tissue diagnosis.

steps.x: **C. Lymph node biopsy.** Suspected Richter's transformation = lymph node biopsy.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has a white cell count of 148 ×10⁹/L (4.0–11.0) with neutrophils, myelocytes and basophils on the film, found after she complained of tiredness and early satiety. Her spleen is palpable 10 cm below the costal margin.
questions.q: Which result would best confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: CML is defined by the t(9;22) translocation (Philadelphia chromosome), which forms the BCR-ABL fusion gene, detected by cytogenetics or PCR.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or confirm before reading the options.

clues: palpable 10 cm below the costal margin
steps.x: Massive spleen, very high WCC with all myeloid stages and basophils.

elim: Seen in AML, not CML.
Seen in polycythaemia vera and other myeloproliferative disorders.
Defines acute promyelocytic leukaemia.
Seen in CLL.

steps.x: **B. BCR-ABL fusion gene on PCR.** CML = t(9;22) Philadelphia chromosome = BCR-ABL.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man has 1 week of nosebleeds and bruising. His blood film shows hypergranular promyelocytes, some containing many Auer rods. His fibrinogen is low and his PT prolonged. A bone marrow sample is sent.
questions.q: Which result would most likely confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: Acute promyelocytic leukaemia is defined by t(15;17), which fuses PML and RARA; it presents with cytopenias, MPO-positive promyelocytes and DIC.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or confirm before reading the options.
Abnormal promyelocytes plus DIC.

elim: Seen in childhood ALL, with a good prognosis.
Shows autoimmune haemolysis.
The MYC translocation of Burkitt lymphoma.
The Philadelphia chromosome of CML.

steps.x: **C. t(15;17) translocation.** APML = t(15;17), PML-RARA.

questions.stem: A 4 year old girl is seen by her GP with 10 days of tiredness, pallor and leg pain. She has petechiae on her chest and the liver and spleen are both palpable. Her temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 130 bpm. No blood test has been done yet.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Arrange a full blood count within 2 weeks
Prescribe oral iron and review in 4 weeks
Reassure and review if she worsens
Refer to paediatrics the same day
questions.e: A child with unexplained petechiae or hepatosplenomegaly needs immediate (same-day) referral to paediatrics for suspected leukaemia.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.

clues: liver and spleen are both palpable
steps.x: Child, marrow failure signs and organomegaly.

elim: Too slow; petechiae with hepatosplenomegaly need immediate assessment.
Leukaemia must be excluded first.
Unsafe; these are red-flag signs.
Must be same-day, not routine.

steps.x: **D. Refer to paediatrics the same day.** Suspected leukaemia in a child = same-day paediatric referral.

questions.stem: A 7 year old boy has acute lymphoblastic leukaemia confirmed on bone marrow biopsy. Cytogenetics show hyperdiploidy and no Philadelphia chromosome. He has no CNS involvement. His pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 104/66 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.e: Confirmed acute leukaemia needs urgent chemotherapy, starting with induction in ALL; hyperdiploidy gives a better prognosis.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.
Confirmed childhood ALL with favourable cytogenetics.

elim: Kept for high-risk or relapsed disease, not first-line favourable ALL.
A TKI for BCR-ABL disease; he has no Philadelphia chromosome.
Has no role in treating ALL.
For early CLL, not acute leukaemia.

steps.x: **C. Induction chemotherapy.** ALL treatment = urgent induction chemotherapy.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman has chronic lymphocytic leukaemia found on a routine blood test. She feels well with no fevers, sweats or weight loss. She has two small cervical nodes and no splenomegaly. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Asymptomatic, low-risk CLL is managed by watch and wait with regular blood counts; treatment starts if symptoms or marrow failure develop.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.
Early CLL, no symptoms, normal Hb and platelets.

elim: Far too toxic for asymptomatic early CLL.
Used in CML, not CLL.
Used in acute leukaemia; treating early CLL does not improve survival.
Has no role here.

steps.x: **E. Watch and wait.** Asymptomatic CLL = watch and wait.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man is having chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukaemia. He is breathless walking to the bathroom and has fresh petechiae and gum oozing. He is afebrile. His pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Supportive care in leukaemia includes red cell and platelet transfusions for symptomatic anaemia and bleeding from marrow failure.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.
Symptomatic anaemia and bleeding with very low counts during chemotherapy.

elim: Used in mild haemophilia A and von Willebrand disease, not marrow failure.
His anaemia is from marrow failure, not iron deficiency.
Treats immune thrombocytopenia, not chemotherapy-induced marrow failure.
Supportive care allows treatment to continue.

steps.x: **D. Red cell and platelet transfusion.** Leukaemia supportive care = transfusions and infection management.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is 9 days after a chemotherapy cycle. She phones the ward with shivers. On arrival her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 102/64 mmHg. Blood cultures have been taken. Her full blood count result will be ready in 2 hours.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Chest X-ray, then decide on antibiotics
Paracetamol and repeat temperature in 4 hours
Wait for the neutrophil count before antibiotics
questions.e: Fever after chemotherapy is neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise: give IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam) within 1 hour, without waiting for the count.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.
Fever at the nadir of chemotherapy, cultures taken, count not back.

elim: Antibiotics must not wait for imaging.
Too weak and too slow for suspected neutropenic sepsis.
Masks the fever and delays treatment.
Treat empirically within 1 hour; do not wait for the count.

steps.x: **B. IV piperacillin-tazobactam now.** Suspected neutropenic sepsis = IV antibiotics within 1 hour, empirically.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman is found to have chronic myeloid leukaemia after a routine blood test. PCR shows the BCR-ABL fusion gene. She has mild splenomegaly. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg. She wants to start treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
questions.e: CML is treated with the tyrosine kinase inhibitor imatinib, which targets the BCR-ABL fusion protein.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.
CML with the target protein confirmed.

elim: Used in acute promyelocytic leukaemia.
An anti-CD20 antibody for B-cell lymphoma and CLL.
Does not treat the disease.
For early CLL; CML is treated.

steps.x: **B. Imatinib.** CML first-line = imatinib (BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitor).

questions.stem: A 67 year old man with acute myeloid leukaemia has had three chest infections in 2 months. His white cell count is 86 ×10⁹/L (4.0–11.0), mostly myeloblasts. His neutrophil count is 0.3 ×10⁹/L (2.0–7.5).
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for his infections despite a high white cell count?
o: Blasts crowd out normal myeloid precursors
The blasts are mature, functioning neutrophils
questions.e: A malignant clone proliferates and fills the marrow, displacing normal myeloid, erythroid and megakaryocytic precursors; the high count is non-functional blasts.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind the finding in the vignette.
High white count, but nearly all blasts and almost no neutrophils.

elim: Immune neutropenia does not explain a marrow full of blasts.
There is no splenomegaly described, and blasts explain it.
Not the mechanism of marrow failure in leukaemia.
Blasts are immature and do not fight infection.

steps.x: **B. Blasts crowd out normal myeloid precursors.** Leukaemia = clonal blasts crowd out the marrow = infection, anaemia, bleeding.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has chronic myeloid leukaemia. Cytogenetics show a shortened chromosome 22 from a reciprocal translocation with chromosome 9. He asks how this causes the leukaemia.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Loss of a tumour suppressor on chromosome 17
questions.e: t(9;22) creates the BCR-ABL fusion gene, which encodes a tyrosine kinase that is always switched on, driving uncontrolled myeloid proliferation.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind the finding in the vignette.
The Philadelphia chromosome.

elim: This is PML-RARA in acute promyelocytic leukaemia.
Describes p53 loss, not the Philadelphia chromosome.
Seen in Burkitt lymphoma with t(8;14).
Causes secondary polycythaemia, not CML.

steps.x: **A. A constitutively active tyrosine kinase.** BCR-ABL = always-on tyrosine kinase = CML; imatinib blocks it.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman has acute promyelocytic leukaemia with t(15;17). Her marrow is packed with promyelocytes, and very few mature neutrophils are seen. She is started on all-trans retinoic acid.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her leukaemia?
questions.e: t(15;17) fuses PML and RARA, blocking normal promyelocyte differentiation so promyelocytes accumulate; retinoic acid overcomes this block.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind the finding in the vignette.
Maturation stops at the promyelocyte stage.

elim: The mechanism of CML.
Explains smudge cells in CLL.
Causes oxidative haemolysis, not leukaemia.
The mechanism of Burkitt lymphoma.

steps.x: **E. PML-RARA fusion blocking promyelocyte maturation.** APML = PML-RARA = block at promyelocyte stage.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man with newly diagnosed acute promyelocytic leukaemia develops bleeding from his cannula sites and a large bruise on his thigh. His PT is 21 s (10–14), fibrinogen 0.6 g/L (1.5–4.0) and D-dimer very high.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his bleeding?
questions.e: The abnormal promyelocytes release procoagulant granule contents, consuming clotting factors and fibrinogen: DIC, which is why APML patients bleed.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind the finding in the vignette.
APML with long PT, low fibrinogen and high D-dimer: DIC.

elim: This is immune thrombocytopenia, with normal clotting.
This is haemophilia A, with a normal PT and fibrinogen.
Would not cause a very high D-dimer this quickly.
Would not lower fibrinogen or raise D-dimer.

steps.x: **D. Promyelocyte granules triggering DIC.** APML = DIC, an emergency.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman has pancytopenia with circulating myeloblasts. The blood film shows pink, needle-shaped inclusions in the cytoplasm of the blasts. The haematologist says these confirm a myeloid lineage.
questions.q: Which is the most likely composition of these inclusions?
questions.e: Auer rods are aggregates of azurophilic, myeloperoxidase-rich granule material in myeloblasts, a hallmark of AML.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind the finding in the vignette.
Rod-shaped inclusions in myeloblasts: Auer rods.

elim: Forms Heinz bodies in red cells.
Form Howell-Jolly bodies in red cells.
Causes basophilic stippling in red cells.
Form smudge cells in CLL.

steps.x: **A. Aggregated myeloperoxidase-rich granules.** Auer rods = clumped MPO-rich azurophilic granules = AML.

questions.stem: A 79 year old man has a lymphocyte count of 31 ×10⁹/L (1.0–4.0). His blood film shows many small mature lymphocytes and numerous ragged cell remnants. Peripheral blood flow cytometry confirms a clonal B-cell population.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the cell remnants?
o: Complement destroys red cells in the blood
Fragile lymphocytes rupture when the film is made
questions.e: Smudge cells in CLL reflect the fragility of the malignant small lymphocytes, which rupture during film preparation; flow cytometry is first-line to confirm CLL.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind the finding in the vignette.
CLL lymphocytosis with smeared remnants on the film.

elim: Causes spherocytes or haemolysis, not lymphocyte remnants.
Causes pseudothrombocytopenia, not ruptured lymphocytes.
Gives bite cells or spherocytes, not smudge cells.
Infection causes atypical lymphocytes, not smudge cells.

steps.x: **B. Fragile lymphocytes rupture when the film is made.** Smudge cells = fragile CLL lymphocytes squashed on the slide.
